newsitem.title: UK: Canada's Gulf blasts Clyde defense.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Gulf blasts Clyde defense.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd hit out Monday at takeover target Clyde Petroleum, saying the British oil company used the wrong method and numbers in its defence against Gulf's 432 million pound ($730 million) offer.
"The logic they used is ... inappropriate and the methodology is unprecedented," Dick Auchinleck, Gulf Canada's senior vice president of international marketing, told Reuters.
He dismissed Clyde's defence, released Sunday, as "thin soup."
"There is no meat in this document at all," he said.
While the two firms were locked in a battle over Clyde's value, Clyde shareholders continued to be optimistic of a higher bid emerging, either from Gulf or a white knight suitor.
In mid-afternoon trading on Monday, Clyde firmed 1/2 a penny to 117 pence but the premium over Gulf Canada's cash offer of 105p per share did not worry Clyde's advisers.
"It is normal at this stage to see the share price above the offer price," said Nigel Meek of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But Colin Smith at BZW saw a reasonable chance of a counter bid emerging at a higher price. "It is unlikely it (Clyde) will go for less than 125 pence," he said.
Auchinleck criticised Clyde for ignoring its net asset value and concentrating instead on its cash flow multiple to defend itself against Gulf Canada's hostile bid, which was launched on Dec. 18.

"NAV is used unfailingly by every single analyst, certainly in this country, and it is also the measure North American companies will use to value other companies," he said. "The cash flow multiple itself is a very short-term valuation measure," Auchinleck added.
He also criticised Clyde, which is active in the North Sea, Australia and Indonesia, for comparing the closing share price on Jan. 3, 1997 with the company's 1995 cash flow.
"That is really unprecedented. Cash flow analysis should really be about the future and not the past," Auchinleck said, adding that Clyde's cash flow was expected to fall in 1998 and 1999.

The net asset value method is used by most British analysts and is based on a company's production from existing oil and gas reserves, ignoring exploration projects that might lead to new production in the future.
Given the long lifetime of oil and gas fields, the net asset value approach has a wider time horizon than the cash flow valuation, which is usually derived from expectations over two to three years.
Analysts using the net asset value method praise its long- term view, allowing for a great variety of adjustable assumptions on such matters as tax and oil price.

Critics, however, claim too many assumptions have to be made to arrive at any firm conclusions. But some cash flow multiple supporters concede that the net value methodology can be useful for analysing small companies such as Clyde.
Gulf Canada does not want to give its estimate of Clyde's net asset value at this stage and Auchinleck also declined to estimate a fair cash flow multiple for the firm.

In its defence document, Clyde said the bid put it on a cash flow multiple of 5.7 times, comparing unfavourably with comparable international companies trading on an historic multiple of 8.9 times and Gulf Canada on 12.7 times.
Analysts' estimates of Clyde's net asset value per share roughly range between 70 and 85 pence.
